The problem

A shop can only bid as many jobs as its estimators can count.

Slow

Count every fixture. Size every pipe. Look up every code. Price every line. Write the letter. Days of a senior person's time, per bid.

Scarce

75,000 estimators for 588,000 shops. Most shops have none, so they never bid plan work at all.

Risky

Every plan set has mistakes. Miss one and the shop pays for it in the field. Catching it takes your most experienced person.

The work goes to whoever gets a good number out first. Today that is whoever has the most estimators.

Estimator and shop counts from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024.

Say the problem in the buyer's words before any product. The bottleneck is people: a bid is days of a senior estimator's time, most shops have no estimator at all, and the mistakes in the plans land on whoever missed them. Everything that follows is the answer to this slide.

What is new

The robot is a user.

1 · It bids first, blind

The robot bids the same job from the same plans and locks its number before the person has one. It cannot copy.

2 · The person bids, then looks

They write down their number, then open the robot's and compare, while the bid can still change.

3 · The app keeps score

When the bid goes out, the difference is written on the bid. A person signs off, fixes what is wrong, or redoes any step by hand.

92–93%

as accurate as a human estimator

Checked two ways: blind bids on live jobs, and re-bids of old jobs we already won or lost. Every score is written on the bid itself, so any one of them can be checked.

The robot has its own login and uses the same screens, price books and notes as a person. Scored on [N] jobs so far; every new bid adds one.

The novelty in one sentence: most "AI estimating" is a black box that emits a number; ours is a workflow a person can do by hand, and the robot does the same workflow, in the open, on the same records. Emphasize the blindness: a shadow bid is refused if the human number is already on record, which is what makes the accuracy figure honest. Say the number as accuracy, not error. Under the hood

Every plan set has mistakes. Someone pays for each one.

You miss it

You bid the drawing as drawn. The mistake shows up in the field, and you eat it.

You pay

You catch it late

You find it after the bid. Now it is a change order fight, rework and delay, and you still pay most of it.

You pay

You catch it before you bid

You expose it in the bid, and the company that sent the plans pays. Until now that took hiring someone smart enough to see it.

They pay

Our apps make catching mistakes standard. Every takeoff gets the same checks: does it add up, is every page scaled, does the drawing break a code rule, is anything counted twice? The mistakes show up before the bid goes out, not after.

This slide is the one an HVAC owner will feel. The third column is where the tools change the economics: catching the plan's mistakes stops being a senior-estimator skill and becomes a standard step the app runs on every takeoff.

Backup · How the robot is scored

How a robot bids alongside a person

1 · Shadow

The robot bids first

The robot bids the same job from the same plans. It locks in its number before the person has one. It cannot copy.

2 · Envelope

The person bids, then looks

The person writes down their number. Then they open the robot's number and compare, while the bid can still change.

3 · Score

The app keeps score

When the bid goes out, the app writes down how far apart the two numbers were. A scoreboard tracks it over time.

4 · Audit

A person checks the robot

A board shows every robot bid and its score. A person signs off, fixes what is wrong, or takes over.

The robot is also graded on old bids we already won or lost, so its score is not one lucky job.

Emphasize the blindness. Shadow bids are refused if the human number is already on record. That is what makes the accuracy figure on the next slide an honest one.

Backup · How a person takes over

Cheap for the robot. Easy for the person.

Counts

Takeoffs

Labor

Pricing

Letter

Why the robot can do it cheaply

  • A bid is five small steps, not one big document.
  • Each step is a screen for a person and one command for a robot.
  • The price books do the pricing. The robot never makes up a price.
  • Each step can be checked on its own: do the counts add up, does every row have a price, does the total match?

Why a person can check it, or take over

  • Every change leaves a note on the bid, in plain words, with who did it.
  • Any step can be redone by hand on the same screen.
  • If the plans are too bad for the robot, the person does that step. The rest still stands.
The key architectural choice: we made bidding by hand so granular and so cheap that a robot can jump in on top of it, and a person can jump back in anywhere without throwing the rest away.
